items.stem: A bank's compliance pipeline classifies 10,000 transaction alerts per day into risk tiers under a 2-second latency budget, and drafts the referral letter language sent to a named regulator whenever a tier triggers escalation. Which model strategy should be used?

opts.t: Use the smallest, fastest model for every step, since the volume and latency budget dominate the task.
Route bulk classification to the fast model, but reserve a higher-capability model for drafting the regulator referral text.
Run the entire pipeline, including bulk classification, on the highest-capability model available, to be safe.
Fine-tune the fast model on past referral letters instead of testing whether a stronger base model suffices.

items.whyRight: The volume and latency budget fit the fast model for bulk classification, but the referral text requires open-ended judgment when addressing a regulator — a rung the fast model's own accuracy bar wasn't built to clear, so that step alone needs the higher-capability model.

whyWrong.A: Volume and latency alone would justify this for pure classification, but the stem's own escalation requirement is an open-ended judgment call this model can't reliably clear.
whyWrong.C: Upgrading bulk classification too adds cost and latency the 2-second budget doesn't have room for, when only the escalation step needs the extra capability.
whyWrong.D: Fine-tuning is the expensive lever; it doesn't test whether a stronger base model already handles regulator-facing drafting without any additional training.

items.t1Clause: drafts the referral letter language sent to a named regulator whenever a tier triggers escalation
items.factAnswerRaw: Route bulk classification to the fast model, but reserve a higher-capability model for drafting the regulator referral text.

items.stem: A subscription service's support-agent system prompt refuses any discussion of account cancellation, correctly blocking retention-abuse requests. A consumer-protection rule now requires the same agent to process cancellations within 48 hours when requested through a dedicated retention tool, with legal sign-off. What should change?

opts.t: Add the exception into the system prompt's top-level guardrail language, so it applies to every tool.
Add a scoped exception to the retention tool's own system prompt, leaving the blanket guardrail in place elsewhere.
Move the cancellation check into client-side validation before requests ever reach the model.
Document the new exception in team onboarding materials, without changing the system prompt itself.

items.whyRight: The blanket guardrail still correctly blocks retention abuse elsewhere, so it should stay; the legitimate need is scoped to one tool, and guardrails belong at the layer where the exception actually applies — a per-tool addition, not a blanket rewrite.

whyWrong.A: The need is scoped to one tool; rewriting the top-level guardrail applies the exception everywhere, undoing protection the guardrail still correctly provides elsewhere.
whyWrong.C: A client-side check never reaches the model itself — the same failure as setting a behavioral rule through an environment variable.
whyWrong.D: Documentation elsewhere in the pipeline never reaches the model as an instruction, so its behavior toward cancellation requests won't change.

items.t1Clause: when requested through a dedicated retention tool
items.factAnswerRaw: Add a scoped exception to the retention tool's own system prompt, leaving the blanket guardrail in place elsewhere.

items.stem: A multi-step reconciliation agent compares entries across 12 ledgers using a step-by-step reasoning cue; a prior test without the cue produced a higher error rate. A product manager proposes dropping the cue now, since responses already return within budget. What should happen?

opts.t: Keep the reasoning cue; the prior test already showed accuracy drops on this task without it.
Drop the cue now that latency is within budget, since token savings outweigh a one-time test result.
Replace the reasoning cue with a bounded scratchpad to cut tokens while preserving most of the accuracy benefit.
Remove the cue, since the task's format looks similar to previous single-step tasks that didn't need one.

items.whyRight: The task is genuinely multi-step, and the cue is already verified necessary: removing it earlier measurably raised the error rate. Nothing in the stem states a latency conflict, so the sophisticated-sounding token-saving proposal would reopen the accuracy failure the cue was added to prevent.

whyWrong.B: The prior test already measured a higher error rate without the cue; token savings don't outweigh evidence the stem itself provides.
whyWrong.C: This targets a latency conflict the stem never states exists; the plain cue already works without needing to be bounded.
whyWrong.D: The task compares entries across 12 ledgers in multiple steps; treating it as single-step misreads its actual shape.

items.t1Clause: since responses already return within budget
items.factAnswerRaw: Keep the reasoning cue; the prior test already showed accuracy drops on this task without it.

items.stem: An HR assistant answers thousands of daily employee queries from a 40-page benefits handbook containing about 30 scattered bullet facts, none more critical than another, and keeps missing facts buried in the middle of the document. What should be changed?

opts.t: Leave the document's structure unchanged, since it's well under the model's effective context window.
Pull the single most business-critical fact into a highlighted block near the top of the handbook.
Convert the scattered bullets into explicit headed sections grouped by topic, even without one dominant fact.
Shorten the handbook to a strict length limit before employee queries reach the model.

items.whyRight: No single fact in the handbook is more critical than another, so the fix is structural, not a top-of-document highlight built for one dominant fact. Headed sections grouped by topic restore retrievability across the whole middle, which a 40-page scattered-bullet document actually needs.

whyWrong.A: A 40-page handbook queried thousands of times a day is exactly the scale the effect occurs at; 'short input' doesn't describe this document.
whyWrong.B: The stem states no fact is more critical than another, so highlighting a single fact targets a problem this handbook doesn't have.
whyWrong.D: Shortening under a length limit risks cutting exactly the scattered facts that are already going missing.

items.factAnswerRaw: Convert to explicit headed sections grouped by topic, even without one findings-first summary.

notes: g15 (F-2.6-02): mapped to the third row of 2.6's new 'Scope of the Fix' table (scattered facts, no single dominant fact -> headed sections grouped by topic) based on content fit against the invGuidance-free slot; FACET-LEDGER.md was not part of this batch's required reading, so exact facet-to-row numbering wasn't independently confirmed against it.

g13 (F-2.2-05, inverted): T1's alt (option A, blanket top-level exception) is grounded in the logical converse of the Guardrail Scope table's stated row (per-layer scoping is needed only when behavior must differ by tool/sub-agent; if the need became uniform across all layers, a blanket rule follows) rather than a row stated in that exact form in the corpus -- flagging for the grounding audit to confirm this converse reading is acceptable rather than treating it as a fabricated row.

g13 (F-2.2-05, inverted): section 2.2's system-prompt-authority rule is close to absolute, as the brief itself flags for this section/shape pairing; the S8 framing (scoped exception vs. removal) was used per invGuidance rather than the section's usual S2 hint, and no IRREDUCIBLE flag was needed since a clean T1 resolution was found (see t1Clause), but this item is a good candidate for extra audit scrutiny given the section's known difficulty.
